paper.abstract:
Abstract Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows.
Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer’s semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed.
We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them.
We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI).
Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively.
Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips.
On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems.
Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: AI agents are increasingly able to carry out user requests by operating software applications on computers directly. Computer-use research has expanded from everyday desktop tasks in OSWorld 1.0 [ 1 ] to long-horizon workflows and specialized professional software in OSWorld 2.0 [ 2 ] . As tasks become more involved, agents must sustain progress across many operations, making interaction efficiency important alongside task performance. Most existing computer-use interfaces mirror how humans operate software: inspect the screen, locate a UI control, and use the mouse or keyboard. While this approach offers broad coverage with human-like perception and action, it also imposes a strong human-interaction prior on the action space of a frontier Large Language Model (LLM), overlooking more efficient channels for interacting directly with the system. An agent with existing computer-use interface may spend substantial effort precisely locating a field by screen coordinates even when the application exposes its identity and value through accessibility data, or manipulate data through repeated click-and-drag actions when code could process it directly. Modern computer systems offer a wide range of interaction tools that fall into three complementary channels: visual interaction through GUIs, structured semantic access through accessibility APIs, and direct programmatic access through code and command-line tools such as Bash. Accessibility (AX), originally developed for assistive technologies and now also used for automation, exposes application UI controls, their properties, and supported operations [ 3 , 4 ] . Code and command-line tools provide direct access to files, data, and software, while GUI interaction supplies visual evidence and control where structured access is insufficient. Prior work [ 5 , 6 ] combines programmatic and visual interaction but makes limited use of the semantic channel provided by AX. UFO2 combines UI Automation with GUI and application-API execution [ 7 ] , while Tactile exposes semantic actions alongside OCR and visual fallbacks [ 8 ] . CUA Driver, an open-source computer-use interface, supports all three channels but favors AX-based interaction in the background to preserve the user’s active desktop [ 9 ] . We build on these efforts to organize reference-addressed AX actions, in-call wait steps, and post-action feedback for efficient, sustained interaction, while exposing all three channels within a general agent for model-directed selection and combination. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction (Figure 1 ). HCU adds AX and GUI tools to the agent’s own programmatic tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with cross-channel action guards to maintain a consistent view of the current desktop state and an HCU skill to guide the model in selecting and combining the exposed channels. Our designed AX channel lets the model read a compact AX view, act on several targets in one call, and see the resulting changes without a separate observation. Because all three channels act on the same desktop, an action in one can invalidate the evidence held by another; action guards therefore re-check targets and layouts against live state before each input. A supplementary HCU skill explains how to use these tools and when each channel is most effective, helping the model follow the execution and feedback contracts and reduce invocation errors. We evaluate HCU on OSWorld 2.0 and OSWorld 1.0, and further evaluate it on WeaveBench, MacAgentBench, and Windows Agent Arena in Appendix A . On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among compared systems, advancing the performance–efficiency frontier (Figure 1 , right). With GPT-6 Astra , it reaches 72.37% Partial, outperforming CUA Driver by 3.55 points. With Claude Opus 5, it improves Partial by 3.75 points and Binary by 3.76 points over the model’s official leaderboard result, reaching 35.19% Binary at 20% lower Cost. On OSWorld 1.0, HCU outperforms CUA Driver across four other backbone models, each in its own harness, averaging 6.48 more points in Score, 17% fewer Steps, and 30% lower Cost, and reaches 70.13% Score with GPT-5.4 while transferring these performance and efficiency gains to WeaveBench, MacAgentBench, and Windows Agent Arena at roughly half the Cost. Component ablations and tool-call analyses reveal distinct channel preferences across models, yet gains consistently concentrate on tasks that use HCU’s desktop tools. Within tasks, we observe that channels often play complementary roles, with screenshots supporting observation and AX enabling execution. The skill helps agents use the interface more reliably, reducing the proportion of AX and GUI calls rejected for malformed arguments from 17.37% to 1.36%. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We introduce HCU, a unified interface for general agents that combines programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction. HCU pairs model-directed channel selection with cross-channel action guards and AX tools for compact observation, batched actions with wait steps, and post-action feedback. 2. We show that HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on OSWorld 2.0 and advances the performance–efficiency frontier, and that it consistently improves both task performance and efficiency over CUA Driver across diverse backbone models, agent harnesses, and desktop platforms. 3. We analyze the ablations and the cross-model comparison at the level of tool calls, showing that models given the same channels divide them differently, and we distill design lessons for future computer-use interfaces.

sections.heading: From GUI-based to hybrid computer use.
sections.text: Most computer-use agents observe screenshots and act through mouse-and-keyboard input. Work in this line improves grounding and planning, for example by routing GUI localization to specialist models and refining plans hierarchically [ 10 ] , and most results reported on OSWorld 1.0 and OSWorld 2.0 come from such screenshot-based loops [ 1 , 2 , 11 ] . Hybrid systems add programmatic access beside this visual loop. Some build dedicated multi-agent systems: CoAct-1 uses an orchestrator to delegate subtasks to a Programmer and a GUI Operator [ 12 ] , and StateAct prioritizes direct program-state access and delegates visual interaction to a GUI subagent [ 13 ] . Others place GUI interaction inside a general agent: the GUI-as-Tool setup in ALE and the desktop plugin evaluated in WeaveBench expose screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions as tools alongside the agent’s programmatic tools [ 5 , 6 ] . While these works are training-free designs built around off-the-shelf models, Mage-VL-Cowork explores hybrid computer use from the training side [ 14 ] . More broadly, SWE-agent shows how agent-computer interface design affects agent behavior and performance in software engineering [ 15 ] . Like ALE and WeaveBench, HCU extends a general agent without model training and leaves the division of work among channels to the model, while adding a semantic channel beside the programmatic and visual ones.

sections.heading: Semantic interaction with computers.
sections.text: Interfaces that expose semantic information differ in how they identify targets and execute actions. The original OSWorld 1.0 set-of-marks baseline uses AX information to identify targets, but maps element identifiers to coordinates for GUI input [ 1 , 16 ] . UFO2 combines UI Automation and visual control detection with GUI and application-API execution [ 7 ] . Tactile exposes compact desktop candidates and semantic actions with OCR and visual fallbacks [ 8 ] . CUA Driver, our baseline, supports element-addressed actions and coordinate input under a best-effort background policy [ 9 ] . In browsers, Playwright MCP provides accessibility snapshots and explicit target references [ 17 ] , while Cocoa-Agent combines DOM queries and element-addressed actions with screenshots and programmatic tools [ 18 ] . HCU uses explicit target references on desktop AX and adds batched AX actions with wait steps in the same call, cross-channel action guards, and AX diffs as post-action feedback.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and efficiency.
sections.text: OSWorld 1.0 is a widely used benchmark for computer-use agents in real desktop environments [ 1 ] , and OSWorld 2.0 extends this evaluation to long-horizon real-world workflows [ 2 ] . Early evaluations centered on GUI interaction; recent benchmarks increasingly examine hybrid workflows and cross-platform desktop use [ 6 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Following cost-aware agent evaluation [ 22 ] , we report task performance together with resource use across OSWorld 2.0, OSWorld 1.0, and the cross-platform evaluations in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Hybrid Computer Use Interface
sections.text: HCU combines three interaction channels in one agent’s task context: programmatic, semantic, and visual (Figure 2 , top). The programmatic channel uses the agent’s own code, shell, and file tools. HCU adds the semantic and visual channels through two desktop tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [ 23 ] : the AX channel reads application accessibility trees and executes reference-addressed actions, while the GUI channel takes screenshots and sends mouse and keyboard input (Appendix Table 13 ). All three channels act on the same computer. Action guards check AX targets and GUI layouts against live state before input. A supplementary skill explains how to use the interface. The agent uses HCU within its existing observation–action loop. Given the task and available observations, the model chooses a channel to inspect state or act; the selected tool executes the request and returns its result to the same context, from which the model decides whether to continue, inspect further, or change channels. Observation and execution need not use the same channel: a screenshot can supply visual context for a subsequent AX action. Channel selection remains model-directed. HCU adds no planner, subagents, or loop of its own, so the same interface attaches to different agent harnesses (Appendix E.5 ). The following subsections describe the AX channel’s observation, execution, and feedback design (Section 3.1 ), the action guards that support switching between channels (Section 3.2 ), and the skill that explains how to use the interface (Section 3.3 ). Figure 2: HCU overview. Top: channels, skill, and action guards. Bottom: a compact AX view, batched actions with a wait step, and the returned effect summary and AX diff.

sections.heading: Accessibility for Computer Control
sections.text: AX exposes a structured representation that applications or UI frameworks supply for assistive technologies: a tree of elements with roles, names, values, states, and supported operations. It lets an agent identify and operate controls without locating every target in pixels, but using it to control a computer presents three challenges. 1. Coverage depends on what applications expose. Applications choose which properties and operations to expose through AX. Custom-drawn content may have no accessible elements, accessible objects need not map one-to-one to widgets, and virtualized items may be absent until rendered [ 3 , 24 ] . AX therefore provides incomplete coverage of visible content and available interactions. CUA Driver addresses this by returning the tree and a screenshot together by default, so the model can use pixels when AX omits or misrepresents a target [ 25 ] . HCU retains the acquired AX records, marks unavailable information, and lets the model request a screenshot when semantic evidence is insufficient. 2. Changing targets. Controls can share names, move, disappear, or be recreated; AT-SPI explicitly marks defunct objects [ 26 ] . A label or tree position therefore cannot establish identity across actions. CUA Driver instructs the agent to refresh element indices before acting and rejects ambiguous window targets [ 27 , 28 ] . HCU binds target references independently of the displayed view and resolves them against live elements before each action, including actions within a batch. 3. Verifying action effects. AT-SPI reports invocation, which does not establish that the intended state change occurred [ 29 ] . CUA Driver verifies caller-defined postconditions through a separate operation [ 27 ] . HCU lets the agent compose actions and optional AX wait steps in one batch, such as selecting a checkbox and waiting for its checked state before continuing, without a separate verification call. CUA Driver prioritizes best-effort background input to preserve the user’s active desktop, with foreground input available on request [ 9 ] . In contrast, HCU prioritizes completing the requested action, using native AX operations or focused input as needed. Its efficiency-oriented design also gives the agent more control over how work is composed: compact views reduce observation size, while batched actions, optional wait steps, and AX diffs let the agent combine execution, verification, and state feedback within a single call.

sections.heading: Composable Semantic Interaction
sections.text: These properties motivate an AX interface that lets the agent compose actions while HCU validates targets, runs requested wait steps, and returns evidence for continuation. Figure 2 (bottom) illustrates this interaction: a compact AX view supplies target references, a batch combines actions with optional wait steps, and post-action feedback supports the next decision.

sections.heading: Compact AX views and target references.
sections.text: HCU separates the AX records it retains from the compact AX view shown to the model. It removes structural wrappers and condenses repeated content in the view while retaining the acquired records for target identification and state comparison. Target references are bound to elements before this compression, so shortening the view does not change which element a reference identifies. The retained records also support AX diffs after an action, while find and scoped observations let the model retrieve targets omitted from the compact AX view. Appendix E.2 gives same-capture examples and measures the reduction in tokens.

sections.heading: Batched actions and wait steps.
sections.text: HCU lets the agent compose known actions and optional AX wait steps in a single call. The act mode executes the steps in order within one application window, checking each target with the AX target guard before input (Section 3.2 ). A wait step sends no input and holds until an expected state appears, such as a checkbox becoming checked or a dialog opening, before later steps run; placed last, it verifies the final state. This combines batching, also used for GUI interaction [ 6 ] , with state verification akin to Playwright assertions [ 30 ] . If an action fails, a wait times out, or window continuity is lost, HCU stops the batch and reports the stopping point and execution evidence. This lets the agent decide how to continue without blindly repeating earlier actions.

sections.heading: Post-action feedback.
sections.text: HCU returns per-target effect summaries and an AX diff by default after an action call, showing changed values, window changes, and target references relative to the last eligible observation delivered to the model. The agent can instead request a screenshot or execution evidence only, according to what it needs for its next decision. Returning this feedback with the action lets the agent continue without a separate observation when the information suffices (traces and samples in Appendix Figure 16 and E.3 ). HCU reports only what the available evidence supports, so the agent is not led to treat input delivery as a verified effect. Like CUA Driver [ 27 ] , it distinguishes known non-delivery from an unknown effect after possible input. The agent uses this distinction and the returned continuation instructions to decide whether to retry, inspect state, or stop.

After an action, it may not know which earlier observations remain valid, especially when combining channels. An AX action may open a dialog over coordinates from an earlier screenshot, or a GUI action may replace a control addressed by an AX reference. Reusing that evidence can send input to an unintended target without the model noticing. HCU therefore leaves channel choice to the model while using action guards to check the targets and layouts on which its actions depend immediately before input (Algorithm 1 ). The AX target guard resolves each target reference immediately before execution and checks the element’s identity and action-specific requirements. If the target is missing, ambiguous, or replaced, or an action-specific requirement is not met, HCU rejects the action without sending input. It does not redirect the action to a similarly named element. The GUI layout guard checks whether the layout underlying the model’s chosen coordinates still matches the last screenshot. Before coordinate input, it compares the current desktop bounds, visible top-level windows, stacking order, active window, and target-point window layout with those associated with that screenshot. If the layout has changed, HCU blocks the affected input and returns a fresh screenshot so the model can choose new coordinates. Both guards inspect current state regardless of which channel changed it, including earlier actions in the same channel. Detected mismatches lead to explicit rejection before input, allowing the model to revise its next action (Appendix E.4 ; recorded rejection in Figure 18 ).

sections.heading: Skill for Effective Interface Use
sections.text: HCU provides a supplementary skill that explains how to choose and compose the interface’s capabilities. We distilled its instructions from recurring mistakes in development trajectories, including malformed arguments and misused target references, following the trajectory-informed refinement of usage instructions in SWE-agent [ 15 ] . The skill addresses three aspects of interaction: (1) Channel capabilities. The skill explains what programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction can provide, including their observation scope and limitations, so the model can decide which channels to use and combine for the task. (2) Efficient interaction. It explains how to use target references, batch known actions with wait steps, and continue from returned feedback, requesting additional observations only when needed. (3) Verification and recovery. It distinguishes input delivery, local UI changes, and task outcomes; explains how to verify saved or applied results; and describes how to recover from stale targets, invocation errors, or insufficient evidence. The skill makes these instructions concrete through rules for common invocation and recovery mistakes, while the tool schemas define argument shapes. It contains no task-specific solutions; Appendix F.2 presents its text. The skill ablation in Section 4.3 shows reduced invocation errors and improved interaction efficiency; Appendix B.1 describes instruction integration.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: The main experiment uses the OSWorld 2.0 full set (0808 release; 2 ), and the ablations and cross-model study use OSWorld 1.0 [ 1 ] ; Appendix B.1 lists the task sets. Appendix A reports additional evaluations across OSWorld 1.0, WeaveBench [ 6 ] , MacAgentBench [ 19 ] , and Windows Agent Arena [ 20 ] .

sections.heading: Models and comparisons.
sections.text: Each model always runs in the same harness: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.4 in Codex, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, Gemini 3.8 Flash in Gemini CLI, and Grok 4.7 in Grok Build. We therefore name configurations by interface and model. In HCU–CUA Driver comparisons, both interfaces use the same harness execution flow and programmatic tools within each model; auxiliary harness features are restricted to focus the comparison on the interface. The main experiment evaluates HCU (GPT-6 Astra) and HCU (Claude Opus 5) at each model’s highest reasoning effort, with CUA Driver (GPT-6 Astra) as the matched baseline and reported results as context. The interface-component ablations use GPT-5.4 (xhigh); the cross-model comparison adds Claude Opus 5.5 (low), Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and Grok 4.7 (xhigh). We gray out the official GPT-6 Astra results since they were evaluated internally on a subset of tasks. Appendix B.1 details all configurations.

sections.heading: Metrics and budgets.
sections.text: We report Partial (mean task score) and Binary (full-credit rate) on OSWorld 2.0 and Score on OSWorld 1.0, along with per-task resource use. The main experiment uses a 500-step limit and the ablations a 100-step limit. We average results across runs within each configuration. Appendix B details the runs, protocols, and metric accounting.

sections.heading: Cross-platform evaluations.
sections.text: With GPT-5.4, the released version of HCU (Appendix A ) also outperforms CUA Driver on WeaveBench (53.25% vs. 46.37%), the MacAgentBench subset (25 vs. 24 of 28 tasks), and Windows Agent Arena (80.86% vs. 71.89%) at 46–51% lower Cost per task.

sections.heading: HCU beats the baseline on every measure.
sections.text: HCU scores 3.29 points higher than the baseline while using 29.80% fewer Steps, 56.85% fewer input tokens, 29.85% less Time, and 55.36% lower Cost. Every component contributes to this efficiency: each one cuts Steps by 11–15%, so the full interface needs the fewest Steps of all configurations. Figure 3: Skill effects.

sections.heading: AX contributes most.
sections.text: AX is the channel HCU adds to GUI-based computer use: it exposes the applications’ control tree as named, reference-addressed targets and returns observed state changes after action batches. Added to the harness’s programmatic tools and the GUI channel, it raises Score by 2.79 points and cuts Steps by 14.08%, input tokens by 10.44%, Time by 12.58%, and Cost by 10.64%, the largest gain of any component in Score, input, Time, and Cost. The GUI channel complements AX primarily through interaction efficiency: removing GUI leaves Score within run-to-run variation while increasing Steps by 12.45% (Appendix C.1 ). AX thus drives the Score gain and most of the resource savings, while GUI saves Steps when visual context or pixel input is required; Section 4.4 shows how the two divide observation and execution.

sections.heading: Execution-centered AX design supports efficient interaction.
sections.text: HCU’s AX channel integrates guarded execution, optional wait steps, and post-action state in one call (Section 3.1.1 ). With only AX and programmatic tools, HCU w/o GUI exceeds CUA Driver by 3.79 points in Score while using 21.06% fewer Steps, 58.33% fewer input tokens, 29.63% less Time, and 56.70% lower Cost. CUA Driver also offers element-addressed actions and separates delivery from effect [ 27 ] , but leaves verification and renewed observation to separate operations. Both interfaces can sequence actions programmatically; HCU builds verification and feedback into the AX call itself.

sections.heading: The skill improves calling reliability and interaction efficiency.
sections.text: With the skill (Section 3.3 ), the share of AX and GUI calls rejected for malformed arguments falls from 17.37% to 1.36%, and the share of task-runs that repeat such rejections on the same tool while varying the arguments falls from 44.69% to 0.37% (Figure 3 ). Feedback selection also changes: 87% of AX action calls omit the observe field, selecting the default AX diff, compared with 0.2% without the skill. GUI input actions decrease from 4.96 to 1.97 per task. These behavioral changes accompany a 14.55% reduction in Steps and a 1.59-point gain in Score (Appendix B.1 ).

sections.heading: HCU improves every model in Score, input, and Cost.
sections.text: Every model scores higher with HCU than with CUA Driver, by 2.94 to 12.90 points, and uses 18–57% fewer input tokens at 8–55% lower Cost (Table 3 ). Steps and Time also decrease for GPT, Gemini, and Grok. For Claude, Steps remain nearly unchanged while Time increases by 6%; we examine the contrasting patterns of desktop use behind its Step count below.

sections.heading: Models use HCU’s channels differently.
sections.text: All four models allocate a larger share of tool calls to HCU’s AX and GUI desktop tools than to CUA Driver (Figure 4 a). Among HCU’s AX and GUI calls, AX accounts for 80% for GPT, 68% for Grok, and 51% for Gemini. Claude instead uses GUI for 94% of these calls (Figure 4 b) and batches actions more often: 58% of its acting calls contain two or more actions, compared with 11–21% for the other models (Figure 4 c).

sections.heading: Models combine observation and execution across channels.
sections.text: GPT, Gemini, and Grok combine visual observation with semantic action within the same task. On 29–31% of the tasks where each model used GUI, all GUI calls were screenshots, while the model executed actions through AX (Appendix D.1 ). In one recorded task, a screenshot confirmed an entered value missing from AX feedback, after which the agent continued acting through AX (Appendix D.1 ). By leaving channel choice to the model, HCU allows observation and execution to use different channels, enabling the model to draw on their complementary capabilities as the task requires. sections.heading: Score gains concentrate on tasks with AX or GUI use.
sections.text: Across all four models, nearly all of the overall Score gain over CUA Driver comes from tasks where HCU makes at least one AX or GUI call (Figure 5 a). We group tasks by whether HCU makes at least one such call in each run and average the groups’ weighted contributions across runs. The group without these calls contributes only − 0.7 -0.7 to +0.1 points to the overall Score difference (Appendix D.2 ).

sections.heading: Overall Steps mask differences in interaction efficiency.
sections.text: On tasks where both configurations invoke their desktop tools (AX or GUI), HCU uses 19–40% fewer Steps across the four models. HCU also invokes desktop tools on more tasks than CUA Driver (Figure 5 b). For Claude, tasks where only HCU invokes desktop tools gain 7.6 points in Score, accompanied by 53% more Steps. This group’s weighted increase largely offsets the savings where both configurations use desktop tools, explaining Claude’s nearly unchanged overall Steps despite its higher Score. Appendix D.2 provides the complete decomposition.

sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: HCU exposes programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction to a general agent and leaves their selection and combination to the model. It achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on OSWorld 2.0, and consistently outperforms CUA Driver in both task performance and efficiency across diverse backbone models, agent harnesses, and desktop platforms. These results suggest that interfaces built on how people operate software, inspecting the screen and using the mouse and keyboard, cost agents both performance and efficiency. Given AX, three of the four models send most of their desktop calls through it (Section 4.4 ). This echoes the bitter lesson [ 35 ] : a strong human-like interface that fixes how the computer is used may limit what increasingly capable models can do with it. The capabilities HCU exposes already exist on standard desktops and require no model retraining. Finally, the AX channel exposes element states that code can read and act on. This makes it possible to treat the desktop as a programmable environment and to bring desktop work into code execution and programmatic tool calling [ 36 ] . HCU’s batched actions with wait steps (Section 3.1.1 ) provide a direct substrate for this composition. We hope this work encourages interfaces that fully leverage what computers already offer to release model capabilities on computer use.

sections.heading: Appendix A Cross-Platform and Additional Benchmark Evaluation
sections.text: The experiments in the main text use the evaluated version of HCU (Appendix B.1 ). Following those experiments, we refined the interface and skill into the released version described in Appendices E and F . This appendix evaluates HCU across additional benchmarks and operating systems (Figure 6 ): OSWorld 1.0 [ 1 ] and WeaveBench [ 6 ] on Linux, a UI-dependent subset of MacAgentBench [ 19 ] on macOS, and Windows Agent Arena [ 20 ] on Windows. Figure 6: Evaluation of HCU across benchmarks and platforms (GPT-5.4). (a) OSWorld 1.0 (Linux, 360 tasks): Score, Cost per task, and tool-call shift from Shell to desktop tools across CUA Driver, evaluated HCU, and released HCU. (b) WeaveBench (Linux, 114 tasks): mean score and Cost per task across Official OpenClaw, CUA Driver, and HCU. (c) MacAgentBench UI-dependent subset (macOS, 28 tasks) and (d) Windows Agent Arena (Windows, 111 tasks): task performance and resource reductions relative to CUA Driver.

sections.text: Relative to evaluated HCU, released HCU raises Score by 4.36 points and the share of full-score tasks by 4.26 points while using 12.4% fewer Steps, 22.6% fewer input tokens, 15.3% less Time, and 20.2% lower Cost per task (Table 4 ). sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: To compare the native macOS backends of HCU and CUA Driver directly, we also evaluate both interfaces on a 28-task subset of MacAgentBench [ 19 ] . Many native macOS applications in MacAgentBench expose AppleScript dictionaries or command-line utilities that allow an agent with Bash access to complete the task without interacting with the graphical interface, leaving no distinction between desktop-tool interfaces. We therefore select 28 tasks across Clock, Safari, System Settings, and Contacts that require operating the graphical interface to complete, providing a direct comparison between HCU and CUA Driver on macOS. Both arms run with GPT-5.4 at xhigh reasoning effort in Codex, with Bash enabled and 100-step and 1,800-second limits per task. sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: On the 28 UI-dependent macOS tasks, HCU completes 25 of 28 tasks (89.3%) compared with 24 of 28 (85.7%) for CUA Driver, while substantially reducing interaction cost across every efficiency metric (Table 6 ). Because these tasks are relatively straightforward for GPT-5.4 (xhigh) under the 100-step limit, the limit rarely binds and both interfaces reach high completion rates; the advantage of HCU therefore manifests primarily in interaction efficiency, consistent with the below-limit regime in Appendix D.3 . HCU cuts mean Time by 37.8% (544.5 s vs. 876.0 s; median − 36.4 % -36.4\% ), Steps by 24.1% (39.61 vs. 52.21), input tokens by 63.0% (1.34M vs. 3.64M), output tokens by 17.2%, and Cost by 51.4% ($0.7245 vs. $1.4899 per task; $20.29 vs. $41.72 total). Across HCU’s 998 tool calls on these tasks, AX accounts for 49.8% (497), Shell for 28.6% (285), and GUI for 21.6% (216), showing that the semantic channel carries half of all tool calls on macOS when tasks require desktop UI interaction.

sections.heading: Appendix B Experimental Setup and OSWorld 2.0 Details
sections.text: This appendix specifies the task sets, agent configurations, metrics, and OSWorld 2.0 comparison details for Section 4 .

sections.heading: Task sets.
sections.text: The main experiment uses the OSWorld 2.0 full set (108 tasks; 0808 release). The OSWorld 1.0 comparisons cover 361 tasks (excluding eight Google Drive tasks): 93 multi-application tasks, 47 each in LibreOffice Calc and Impress, 46 in Chrome, 26 in GIMP, 24 operating-system tasks, 23 each in VS Code and LibreOffice Writer, 17 in VLC, and 15 in Thunderbird.

sections.heading: Models, harnesses, and tool exposure.
sections.text: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.4 run in Codex; Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5 run in Claude Code; Gemini 3.8 Flash runs in Gemini CLI; and Grok 4.7 runs in Grok Build. The main experiment evaluates GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at each model’s highest reasoning effort under a 500-step limit. The OSWorld 1.0 comparisons use GPT-5.4 (xhigh), Claude Opus 5.5 (low), Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and Grok 4.7 (xhigh) under 100-step and 1,800-second limits per task on isolated Linux desktops. Within each harness, auxiliary features (web search, memory, subagents, and planning modes) are disabled so that both HCU and CUA Driver share the same execution loop, base policy, and programmatic tools (Bash and file tools), with foreground desktop input enabled on all calls. sections.heading: Metrics and aggregation.
sections.text: For task scores s i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] s_{i}\in[0,1] , OSWorld 1.0 Score and OSWorld 2.0 Partial denote the mean score Q mean = 100 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N s i Q_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i} , and OSWorld 2.0 Binary denotes the full-credit rate 100 N ∑ i = 1 N 𝟏 [ s i = 1 ] \frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}=1] . Efficiency is measured by delivered model responses (“Steps”), recorded tool calls, input and output tokens, agent execution Time, and Cost at provider list prices. One model response may issue multiple tool calls, and one AX or GUI call may execute a batch of steps. For configurations with multiple runs (three runs for all five GPT-5.4 ablation configurations, totaling 5,415 task-runs, and two runs for Claude Opus 5.5 HCU), metrics are averaged within each task before averaging across tasks; relative changes are ratios of per-task means.

sections.heading: Evaluated and released versions.
sections.text: The experiments in Section 4 use the evaluated version of HCU, which shares the same channels, target references, action guards, batching, and post-action diffs as the released version. In the released version (Appendices E and F ), in-batch checks are unified as ordered wait steps (replacing action- and batch-level postconditions and assert_ax ), window discovery uses apps (replacing observation_target ), the batch limit increases from 32 to 64 steps, and every AX and GUI result starts with a JSON evidence line carrying a public error code. The released version also adds GUI zoom , AX select , settle waits, the per-target effect report, and per-target-point layout checks on Linux. Appendix A evaluates the released version across OSWorld 1.0, WeaveBench, MacAgentBench, and Windows Agent Arena.

sections.heading: Appendix E HCU Design and Implementation
sections.text: This appendix details HCU’s runtime boundary, AX observation and projection pipeline, batched execution and post-action feedback, cross-channel state guards, and native platform backends.

sections.heading: Interface and System Boundary
sections.text: Table 13 summarizes the public operations of the AX and GUI tools. Programmatic tools (shell, code, and file operations) reside in the agent harness, while the HCU service supplies the semantic and visual desktop operations and their shared state. Table 13: Desktop operations and main request fields. Operation Main request fields Returned evidence and use AX apps No target List top-level windows as wN with title, application, and focus. AX observe app or window_ref ; scope , root Return a compact window tree with state and rN references for subsequent calls. AX find app or window_ref , query , scope ; or cursor Retrieve matching targets and local context without reading an entire window tree. AX act Up to 64 ordered actions and wait steps; observe Execute steps in order, stop at the first failed step, and report per-target effects, window changes, and post-action observation. GUI observation actions with a single screenshot or zoom Return the full-desktop frame, binding its window layout for subsequent coordinate checks, or an enlarged region of that frame. GUI input Up to 64 ordered actions : pointer, drag, scroll, text, keys, or wait Execute mouse and keyboard input against the frame-bound layout and return the final screenshot.

sections.heading: Session ownership and runtime boundary.
sections.text: One process owns one desktop session (Figure 13 ): either the stdio server computer-use mcp , or a background daemon shared by the CLI, the Python SDK, and computer-use mcp --attach , so target references and the input lock persist across entry points. The shared Go service validates calls and maintains AX snapshots, reference registries, find cursors, eligible diff snapshots, and the GUI layout lease. Platform providers implement tree acquisition and native input behind a typed private protocol, while the evaluation runner remains external to HCU. Figure 13: HCU interface and MCP server boundaries. HCU unifies programmatic, semantic, and visual channels; the HCU MCP server provides the AX and GUI tools over a shared Go service, while programmatic tools live in the agent and the evaluation runner remains external. Platform backends: Figure 19 .

sections.heading: References, scope, and projection.
sections.text: The service maintains short references for applications ( aN ), logical top-level windows ( wN ), and elements ( rN ). Element actions resolve these references against live state rather than tree line numbers or display labels; activate and close also accept a window-title substring resolved to a unique wN before input. Window scope defaults to the full window including chrome, whereas content scope selects the primary content surface and root narrows an observation to a subtree. From the provider’s acquired records (roles, names, values, states, actions, geometry, and relations), HCU builds a typed internal tree, binds target references, and projects the compact AX view shown to the model. Projection removes empty structural wrappers, merges adjacent unreferenced text leaves, deduplicates relation-backed labels, preserves context needed to disambiguate same-name controls, displays table cell values alongside names, and summarizes repetitive sibling runs under a structural budget. Because references are bound before projection, omitting a subtree from the displayed view does not invalidate its acquired records, which remain searchable via find .

sections.heading: Same-capture AX views and stock XML comparison.
sections.text: To measure the token reduction from projection alone, we compare the delivered compact AX view against an unpruned rendering of the same acquired records across Chrome (container pruning), Audacity (label deduplication), and Obsidian (Figure 14 ). Projection reduces view tokens by 44.1% in Chrome (1,817 to 1,016 tokens), 14.1% in Audacity (439 to 377), and 12.6% in Obsidian (1,374 to 1,201) while retaining 100% of issued target references (53/53, 11/11, and 48/48). Compared against the stock OSWorld 2.0 /accessibility XML on the same Obsidian window, the full representation drops from 30,526 tokens to 1,237 tokens (Figure 15 ). Figure 14: Same-capture AX excerpts (‘o200k_base‘). Counts cover complete view bodies, excluding headers and images; projection retains all issued references. Figure 15: Obsidian screenshot, stock OSWorld 2.0 XML, and compact AX excerpts.

sections.heading: Batched steps, wait steps, and feedback.
sections.text: An AX act call executes up to 64 ordered actions and wait steps within one logical window. A wait step sends no input and holds until a window title appears, a query matches, a referenced element reaches an expected value, state, or text, a target disappears ( gone ), or the UI changes and stops changing ( settle ). A select step selects an element, substring, or range between two references ( ref to to_ref ) and reports the resulting selection. Action errors, wait timeouts, or window changes stop the batch immediately and report how many steps completed. By default ( observe=diff ), an act call reports a per-target effect: line and a windows: line (opened, closed, or focused wN ), followed by the structured AX diff against the last eligible snapshot delivered to the model. Every AX and GUI response starts with a JSON evidence line carrying a public error code on failure (such as invalid_argument , stale_ref , gui_frame_stale , wait_timeout , window_changed , or effect_unknown ), a corrected call hint, and whether input was emitted. Figure 16 illustrates a recorded AX batch followed by find and continuation. Figure 16: Recorded AX interaction with GPT-5.6 Sol on OSWorld 2.0. The search batch returns the entered value, and a subsequent find supplies the next target.

sections.heading: Cross-channel invalidation and action guards.
sections.text: Figure 17 summarizes how HCU maintains consistency across channels. GUI input that may mutate desktop state invalidates the AX working snapshot, hidden-element cache, and find cursors while retaining reference registries and the last delivered diff snapshot. Conversely, a GUI screenshot or an AX full / screenshot observation registers the current GUI frame and its GUI layout lease. Before each AX action, the target guard resolves the reference against live state and rejects missing, ambiguous, or replaced elements ( stale_ref ). Before each GUI coordinate action, the layout guard checks that the live window layout at the target points still matches the layout lease; on mismatch, it blocks input with gui_frame_stale and returns a fresh screenshot (recorded example in Figure 18 ). If focus or pointer preparation fails in an uncertain state where a queued OS request may still fire, HCU stops desktop automation rather than replaying the batch. Figure 17: Cross-channel state and action guards. GUI mutation invalidates working observations while retaining identities and eligible diff snapshots. The GUI guard checks window layout before coordinate input, and uncertain preparation stops the batch. Figure 18: Recorded Writer layout-guard interaction, HCU (GPT-5.4), OSWorld 1.0. The GUI batch is rejected before input and returns a fresh screenshot; the first two crops share region and scale. Retrying with revised pixel coordinates dispatches seven actions.

sections.heading: Platform Backends and Agent Integration
sections.text: HCU provides native backends for Linux, macOS, and Windows behind the same public AX and GUI contract (Figure 19 ). The shared Go service owns AX representation, reference binding, batch orchestration, wait steps, and diffs, while platform providers execute native checks, tree collection, and input: Python with AT-SPI and X11 on Linux (automatically enabling the session accessibility bus), Swift with AXUIElement, CoreGraphics, ScreenCaptureKit, and SkyLight on macOS, and C# with UIA3 and Win32 on Windows. The binary selects its backend at build time. Standalone configuration generators and evaluation integrations register HCU alongside the built-in tools of Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Grok Build, injecting the base policy and selected skill through each harness’s native context mechanism (Appendix B.1 ). Appendix A evaluates HCU across Linux, macOS, and Windows benchmarks. Figure 19: Shared HCU MCP server and native backends. Rows show capabilities, not a fixed workflow; AX can also return screenshots, and its wait steps are optional. Dashed branches are alternative backends, one selected per build, while the agent’s programmatic tools remain in the harness.

sections.heading: Appendix F Tool Definitions and Skill
sections.text: This appendix reproduces HCU’s server instructions, AX and GUI tool descriptions, base policy ( instructions/base.md ), and hybrid skill ( instructions/hybrid.md ), followed by the two GUI action vocabularies compared in Appendix C.3 .

sections.heading: Server Instructions and Tool Definitions
sections.text: Server instructions Two tools for the running desktop. AX reads and operates application windows through accessibility: it lists windows, returns controls as rN refs, acts on them, and waits with wait steps. GUI takes full-desktop screenshots and sends pixel input. Use AX for named controls, values, menus, dialogs, windows, and keys. Use GUI for pixels, canvases, dragging, and controls that AX does not expose; after one targeted AX find misses a visible control, use GUI for it. Send all desktop input (window activation, keys, text, mouse) through these tools, not shell input utilities or scripted accessibility calls: the tools check the target window before input and report what changed, and outside input makes their refs and diffs stale. After GUI input, read AX again before reusing refs. AX tool description Accessibility for application windows. Modes: apps lists confirmed windows (wN, title, app, active) and reports incomplete inventories; missing windows then remain unknown. observe returns the window tree with rN refs. find returns matching rN. act runs ordered steps, checks them before input, stops at the first failed step, and reports each target’s change, windows opened/closed/focused, and a diff. Copy rN/wN exactly; stale refs fail. keypress/type without ref go to the focused window. select marks ref, its text substring, or ref..to_ref (paragraphs, cells) and reports the selection read back. activate/close take a title substring or wN. A wait step sends no input and fails the batch on timeout: window (title, any app), query (as find), ref with value/state/text, or text; gone inverts. settle needs no prediction: it waits until the UI changes after the step before it and stops changing; it fails only if nothing changed. After a window wait, keys go to that window, after settle to the focused one. Skip waits the report answers. Errors return code and hint. Examples: {"mode":"act","actions":[{"type":"click","ref":"r12"},{"type":"wait","window":"Export"},{"type":"type","text":"q3.csv"},{"type":"keypress","keys":["ENTER"]}]} {"mode":"find","window_ref":"w2","query":{"role":"button","name_contains":"Save"}} GUI tool description Full-desktop screenshot and pixel input. {"actions":[{"type":"screenshot"}]} alone observes; {"type":"zoom","region":[x0,y0,x1,y1]} alone enlarges a frame region to read small text and icons. Any other batch is checked before input and returns one final screenshot. x/y are pixels of the latest full-desktop image (screen width x height) from GUI or AX full/screenshot, which return the same frame. type/keypress go to the current focus, so click the field first. Batch the actions planned from one screenshot; end the batch after an action that may open, close, or move a window, and plan the rest from the returned image. GUI cannot address windows; AX activates and closes them by title. wait is one second with no observation, at most 20 s per batch. Errors return code and hint like AX; gui_frame_stale means nothing was sent: replan from the returned screenshot. Example: {"actions":[{"type":"click","x":640,"y":412},{"type":"type","text":"hello"},{"type":"keypress","keys":["ENTER"]}]}

sections.heading: Base Policy and Skill
sections.text: The instruction package separates common computer-use policy in instructions/base.md from interaction guidance in instructions/hybrid.md . Companion files ( ax-only.md , gui-only.md , and hybrid-code.md ) adapt the same rules to single-channel ablations and code-mode harnesses. Base policy ( instructions/base.md ) # Computer-Use Principles Complete the user’s instruction end to end. Inspect real state, act within the requested scope, and verify the delivered result. For actionable tasks, carry the work through execution rather than stopping at a proposal. Keep progress and final replies concise. ## Scope And Safety - Any general-purpose route may achieve an outcome-only request. Honor an explicitly exclusive method, a method that is itself the user’s purpose, and requirements about visible state. Naming an application does not by itself exclude an equivalent route; "leave the page open" requires the open page. - Preserve unrelated data. Before recursive deletion, moves, overwrites, or permission changes, resolve the absolute targets and preview them. - Never fabricate output, files, application state, screenshots, or verification. Do not read benchmark task definitions, dataset configuration, evaluator or gold internals, hidden checks, other tasks’ traces, or task-derived memory, even when reachable. - Before publishing, sending, or uploading, inspect the outgoing set for secrets without printing them. Remove exposed secrets only when authorized; if safe publication conflicts with preserving the source, ask. - Ask only for information that the user alone can supply and that changes scope, safety, or an irreversible external result. Inspect evidence first, bundle questions, and use the configured reply channel. When the user invites questions and a category, range, or eligibility rule stays ambiguous, ask before the affected external action. For classification or aggregation, account for every source item and recompute dependent results after clarification. ## Who Owns The State - An application that has a document open owns it. It shows its own copy and writes that copy on save, which overwrites edits made to the file elsewhere. Prefer changing an open document in that application and saving it there. If the application cannot reach a needed property, save and close the document (or confirm it has no unsaved changes), edit the file with a format-aware library, parse it, and reopen it. - Change the object the user refers to. Edit it in place and keep its format; create a new file only when asked. - Persist the result the way the user would: save edited documents, confirm settings dialogs, submit forms. Do not overwrite an original the user asked to keep. "Default" and "preference" mean application or user settings unless the user limits them to one object. ## Batch Known Actions - Batch actions whose targets and inputs are already known and whose later steps do not need an intermediate result. Split at the next decision that needs fresh evidence; the maximum batch size is a limit, not a goal. - Combine related shell checks or known command sequences in one call. Check exit status before dependent commands and stop them on failure. Run commands concurrently only when they are independent and do not change shared state. ## Evidence By Result Type | Result | Evidence | | --- | --- | | A file | Parse the saved file | | An exact value in an application | Read the value back from the application | | Appearance, layout, or an image | A full-size screenshot | | A setting or default | The effective setting after a reread, or a newly created object | | A web change | Reload and see the page or record | | A behavior | Exercise it once | | Something the user should see | The window as the user will see it | - Accepted input is not evidence. After the last change, get evidence for each requirement. A check returned by the changing call counts; add another channel only for a requirement it does not cover or when sources conflict. - Stop when every requirement has evidence of its kind in the table. Do not demonstrate the result beyond that evidence: no extra test inputs, restarts, or feature tours. Clean up only temporary state you created that affects the result. Report limitations. One failed channel is not a blocker while another channel can do the work. Hybrid skill ( instructions/hybrid.md ) # Hybrid Computer Use Channels: the shell (commands, scripts, format-aware libraries), the running browser’s automation endpoint when it exposes one, and the ‘AX‘ and ‘GUI‘ tools. The tool descriptions give call shapes. This guide says which channel fits which state, and how to combine them. ## Route By Where The State Lives | State to change | Change it through | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | Files that no running application holds open: data, code, configuration, structured documents, archives, media | Shell with a format-aware library or CLI; check the real format first | Exact, scriptable, and verifiable by parsing | | A document an application holds open | That application: AX for menus, dialogs, and fields; GUI for what AX lacks. For a property neither reaches, save and close it, then edit the file as above | Its copy is what gets saved | | Application or system settings | The settings UI through AX; the configuration file or CLI only when the application is closed or rereads it | A running application can write its cached settings back | | Web pages, forms, signed-in sites | The open browser session: its endpoint if exposed, otherwise AX or GUI | Login, cookies, and tabs exist only in that session | | Canvases, images, drawings, layout | The editor: AX for menus and dialogs, GUI for pixels and dragging | Visual objects have no names to address | | Messages, mail, calendar items, accounts | The client application through AX | The client owns sending and sync | - A documented automation endpoint that a running application already exposes, such as a browser debugging port, acts inside that application. Probe for it once, early. After one failed probe, use AX or GUI. Do not rebuild a site with shell HTTP requests, and do not start another browser or profile: neither shares the user’s session, so their changes do not appear there. - When a setting, property, or command name is known, change it directly. Otherwise learn it from the application: its menus and dialogs, or one narrow query of its help or manual. Do not dump whole help texts or scan binaries and system directories. Search the web only for facts the machine cannot supply; web pages often describe another version. ## Work Efficiently - ‘apps‘ may report an incomplete inventory when an application does not answer. Use confirmed refs from that listing. Missing windows remain unknown; do not infer that they closed or that a title match is unique. - Once the source, target, and operation are known, act. Further checks must answer a concrete blocker. - Plan from one read. After ‘observe‘ or ‘find‘, put every action you can already determine for that window into one ‘act‘, while later refs and focus remain valid. Split when the next action needs a new observation. - Every ‘act‘ result starts with what happened, then a diff: ‘‘‘text effect: r58 checkbox "Interface" checked=false→true windows: opened w5 "Insert Sheet" (dialog, focused) ‘‘‘ ‘effect‘ gives each target’s changed fields, ‘no visible change‘, or ‘unknown‘ with the reason. ‘(only state flags changed in this window)‘ means no page, content, or window changed; if the control should have switched something, the application did not respond. ‘windows‘ names windows that opened, closed, or took focus, with a ‘wN‘ you can use at once. When these lines already show the result, do not read or wait again. Continue from the diff for other changes; read again only when the next decision needs more. - One ‘act‘ can mix actions and ‘wait‘ steps; the first failed step stops the batch. Add a ‘wait‘ only when a later step needs a state that may arrive after the action returns: a slow dialog, a menu item, a value computed later. A checkbox that shows ‘checked=false→true‘, or a dialog listed as ‘opened‘, needs no wait. - Wait for a known state with ‘window‘, ‘query‘, ‘ref‘, or ‘text‘. When you know the UI will change but not what it becomes, such as the exact title of the next dialog, use ‘{"type":"wait","settle":true}‘. It waits until the UI changes and then stops changing, names what changed, and fails with "no change" only when nothing changed. Keys after it go to the window that took focus. Give a slow operation a longer ‘timeout_ms‘. ‘‘‘json {"mode":"act","actions":[{"type":"click","ref":"r12"},{"type":"wait","window":"Export"},{"type":"type","text":"q3.csv"},{"type":"keypress","keys":["ENTER"]},{"type":"wait","window":"Export","gone":true}]} {"mode":"act","actions":[{"type":"click","ref":"r7"},{"type":"wait","query":{"role":"menu item","name_contains":"Paragraph"}},{"type":"click","ref":"r9"}]} ‘‘‘ - Select text or cells with a ‘select‘ step before a command that applies to the selection: ‘{"type":"select","ref":"r4","to_ref":"r5"}‘ selects from paragraph ‘r4‘ through paragraph ‘r5‘, or the cell range between two cells; ‘"text"‘ selects one substring of ‘ref‘. The result reports what is now selected; check it before applying the command. - Take a GUI screenshot when the question is visual or AX lacks a visible element. Do not alternate screenshots and AX reads of an unchanged state. An AX ‘observe:"full"‘ image is the same full-desktop GUI frame; plan GUI coordinates from it without another screenshot. A GUI ‘zoom‘ enlarges a frame region to read small text or icons; click with the frame pixels its mapping gives. - Put GUI actions determined from the same screenshot into one ‘actions‘ array when focus and target positions remain valid. A call returns only a final screenshot. End the batch when a window or dialog opens, closes, moves, resizes, switches, or navigates; use the returned screenshot to plan subsequent coordinates. A screenshot action must stand alone. - On Linux, start a GUI application from the shell with ‘setsid -f APP ARGS >/tmp/APP.log 2>&1 </dev/null‘. Some agent shells kill the process group of each command when it returns; an application started there with ‘&‘, ‘nohup‘, or ‘disown‘ dies without showing a window. - On macOS, use ‘open -a APP‘ to launch through LaunchServices. Reuse an existing application instance and verify its window before sending input. ## When Something Fails Every AX and GUI error starts with a ‘code‘, a recovery ‘hint‘, and whether input was sent. Read ‘failure_code‘, ‘input_emitted‘, ‘completed‘, and ‘retry_same_request‘ when present. If input was sent or ‘completed‘ is nonzero, inspect state and send only what remains. Never repeat the request when ‘retry_same_request=false‘. Next step by code: - ‘invalid_argument‘: nothing was sent. Fix the field named in ‘path‘ as the hint shows. The control is not missing. - ‘stale_ref‘: drop every ref from that result. Use refs from a newer result, or one fresh ‘find‘. - ‘window_changed‘: the batch stopped after ‘completed‘ actions. Read the returned state and send only what remains. - ‘wait_timeout‘: the batch stopped at that ‘wait‘; the steps before it ran and none after it. The message says what was seen instead, or that the state could not be read. Read the returned state and revise the plan; do not resend the same batch. - ‘effect_unknown‘: input may have been sent. Inspect state before any retry, so that nothing is applied twice. - ‘ambiguous_window‘, ‘window_not_found‘: choose a ‘wN‘ from the listed windows. - ‘no_focused_window‘: start the batch with ‘activate‘. - ‘app_unavailable‘: if the application is still starting, wait once for its window with ‘{"mode":"act","actions":[{"type":"wait","window":"..."}]}‘; otherwise use GUI for it. - ‘permission_denied‘: restore the provider’s operating-system permissions and restart it before observing again. Repeating a screenshot cannot grant access. If earlier input was sent, inspect state before sending more. - ‘runtime_error‘: use the specific failure reason. For a temporary read failure, retry the read once unless the result forbids retrying. Inspect current state before retrying input. For ‘coordinate_target_unverified‘, take a GUI screenshot and inspect covering windows and the target; refreshing refs alone does not fix screen-point ownership. - A zero-result find or a timed-out wait may list nearby elements or window refs. Check those suggestions against the intended target before retrying. - ‘gui_frame_stale‘: the window under a GUI coordinate changed after its screenshot, so nothing was sent. Plan again from the returned screenshot. A stop response ends desktop automation: report the uncertainty and stop. After two attempts on the same hypothesis without new evidence, change the mechanism or the channel. Do not nudge coordinates, add Enter, add waits, or relaunch applications to escape uncertainty.

Figure 1: Left: HCU’s programmatic, semantic, and visual channels. Right: OSWorld 2.0 results. Stars mark HCU and the staircase marks the Pareto frontier, detailed in Section 4.2 . Abstract Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer’s semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination. Introduction AI agents are increasingly able to carry out user requests by operating software applications on computers directly. Computer-use research has expanded from everyday desktop tasks in OSWorld 1.0 [ 1 ] to long-horizon workflows and specialized professional software in OSWorld 2.0 [ 2 ] . As tasks become more involved, agents must sustain progress across many operations, making interaction efficiency important alongside task performance. Most existing computer-use interfaces mirror how humans operate software: inspect the screen, locate a UI control, and use the mouse or keyboard. While this approach offers broad coverage with human-like perception and action, it also imposes a strong human-interaction prior on the action space of a frontier Large Language Model (LLM), overlooking more efficient channels for interacting directly with the system. An agent with existing computer-use interface may spend substantial effort precisely locating a field by screen coordinates even when the application exposes its identity and value through accessibility data, or manipulate data through repeated click-and-drag actions when code could process it directly. Modern computer systems offer a wide range of interaction tools that fall into three complementary channels: visual interaction through GUIs, structured semantic access through accessibility APIs, and direct programmatic access through code and command-line tools such as Bash. Accessibility (AX), originally developed for assistive technologies and now also used for automation, exposes application UI controls, their properties, and supported operations [ 3 , 4 ] . Code and command-line tools provide direct access to files, data, and software, while GUI interaction supplies visual evidence and control where structured access is insufficient. Prior work [ 5 , 6 ] combines programmatic and visual interaction but makes limited use of the semantic channel provided by AX. UFO2 combines UI Automation with GUI and application-API execution [ 7 ] , while Tactile exposes semantic actions alongside OCR and visual fallbacks [ 8 ] . CUA Driver, an open-source computer-use interface, supports all three channels but favors AX-based interaction in the background to preserve the user’s active desktop [ 9 ] . We build on these efforts to organize reference-addressed AX actions, in-call wait steps, and post-action feedback for efficient, sustained interaction, while exposing all three channels within a general agent for model-directed selection and combination. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction (Figure 1 ). HCU adds AX and GUI tools to the agent’s own programmatic tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with cross-channel action guards to maintain a consistent view of the current desktop state and an HCU skill to guide the model in selecting and combining the exposed channels. Our designed AX channel lets the model read a compact AX view, act on several targets in one call, and see the resulting changes without a separate observation. Because all three channels act on the same desktop, an action in one can invalidate the evidence held by another; action guards therefore re-check targets and layouts against live state before each input. A supplementary HCU skill explains how to use these tools and when each channel is most effective, helping the model follow the execution and feedback contracts and reduce invocation errors. We evaluate HCU on OSWorld 2.0 and OSWorld 1.0, and further evaluate it on WeaveBench, MacAgentBench, and Windows Agent Arena in Appendix A . On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among compared systems, advancing the performance–efficiency frontier (Figure 1 , right). With GPT-6 Astra , it reaches 72.37% Partial, outperforming CUA Driver by 3.55 points. With Claude Opus 5, it improves Partial by 3.75 points and Binary by 3.76 points over the model’s official leaderboard result, reaching 35.19% Binary at 20% lower Cost. On OSWorld 1.0, HCU outperforms CUA Driver across four other backbone models, each in its own harness, averaging 6.48 more points in Score, 17% fewer Steps, and 30% lower Cost, and reaches 70.13% Score with GPT-5.4 while transferring these performance and efficiency gains to WeaveBench, MacAgentBench, and Windows Agent Arena at roughly half the Cost. Component ablations and tool-call analyses reveal distinct channel preferences across models, yet gains consistently concentrate on tasks that use HCU’s desktop tools. Within tasks, we observe that channels often play complementary roles, with screenshots supporting observation and AX enabling execution. The skill helps agents use the interface more reliably, reducing the proportion of AX and GUI calls rejected for malformed arguments from 17.37% to 1.36%. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We introduce HCU, a unified interface for general agents that combines programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction. HCU pairs model-directed channel selection with cross-channel action guards and AX tools for compact observation, batched actions with wait steps, and post-action feedback. 2. We show that HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on OSWorld 2.0 and advances the performance–efficiency frontier, and that it consistently improves both task performance and efficiency over CUA Driver across diverse backbone models, agent harnesses, and desktop platforms. 3. We analyze the ablations and the cross-model comparison at the level of tool calls, showing that models given the same channels divide them differently, and we distill design lessons for future computer-use interfaces. Related Work From GUI-based to hybrid computer use. Most computer-use agents observe screenshots and act through mouse-and-keyboard input. Work in this line improves grounding and planning, for example by routing GUI localization to specialist models and refining plans hierarchically [ 10 ] , and most results reported on OSWorld 1.0 and OSWorld 2.0 come from such screenshot-based loops [ 1 , 2 , 11 ] . Hybrid systems add programmatic access beside this visual loop. Some build dedicated multi-agent systems: CoAct-1 uses an orchestrator to delegate subtasks to a Programmer and a GUI Operator [ 12 ] , and StateAct prioritizes direct program-state access and delegates visual interaction to a GUI subagent [ 13 ] . Others place GUI interaction inside a general agent: the GUI-as-Tool setup in ALE and the desktop plugin evaluated in WeaveBench expose screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions as tools alongside the agent’s programmatic tools [ 5 , 6 ] . While these works are training-free designs built around off-the-shelf models, Mage-VL-Cowork explores hybrid computer use from the training side [ 14 ] . More broadly, SWE-agent shows how agent-computer interface design affects agent behavior and performance in software engineering [ 15 ] . Like ALE and WeaveBench, HCU extends a general agent without model training and leaves the division of work among channels to the model, while adding a semantic channel beside the programmatic and visual ones. Semantic interaction with computers. Interfaces that expose semantic information differ in how they identify targets and execute actions. The original OSWorld 1.0 set-of-marks baseline uses AX information to identify targets, but maps element identifiers to coordinates for GUI input [ 1 , 16 ] . UFO2 combines UI Automation and visual control detection with GUI and application-API execution [ 7 ] . Tactile exposes compact desktop candidates and semantic actions with OCR and visual fallbacks [ 8 ] . CUA Driver, our baseline, supports element-addressed actions and coordinate input under a best-effort background policy [ 9 ] . In browsers, Playwright MCP provides accessibility snapshots and explicit target references [ 17 ] , while Cocoa-Agent combines DOM queries and element-addressed actions with screenshots and programmatic tools [ 18 ] . HCU uses explicit target references on desktop AX and adds batched AX actions with wait steps in the same call, cross-channel action guards, and AX diffs as post-action feedback. Benchmarks and efficiency. OSWorld 1.0 is a widely used benchmark for computer-use agents in real desktop environments [ 1 ] , and OSWorld 2.0 extends this evaluation to long-horizon real-world workflows [ 2 ] . Early evaluations centered on GUI interaction; recent benchmarks increasingly examine hybrid workflows and cross-platform desktop use [ 6 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Following cost-aware agent evaluation [ 22 ] , we report task performance together with resource use across OSWorld 2.0, OSWorld 1.0, and the cross-platform evaluations in Appendix A . Hybrid Computer Use Interface HCU combines three interaction channels in one agent’s task context: programmatic, semantic, and visual (Figure 2 , top). The programmatic channel uses the agent’s own code, shell, and file tools. HCU adds the semantic and visual channels through two desktop tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [ 23 ] : the AX channel reads application accessibility trees and executes reference-addressed actions, while the GUI channel takes screenshots and sends mouse and keyboard input (Appendix Table 13 ). All three channels act on the same computer. Action guards check AX targets and GUI layouts against live state before input. A supplementary skill explains how to use the interface. The agent uses HCU within its existing observation–action loop. Given the task and available observations, the model chooses a channel to inspect state or act; the selected tool executes the request and returns its result to the same context, from which the model decides whether to continue, inspect further, or change channels. Observation and execution need not use the same channel: a screenshot can supply visual context for a subsequent AX action. Channel selection remains model-directed. HCU adds no planner, subagents, or loop of its own, so the same interface attaches to different agent harnesses (Appendix E.5 ). The following subsections describe the AX channel’s observation, execution, and feedback design (Section 3.1 ), the action guards that support switching between channels (Section 3.2 ), and the skill that explains how to use the interface (Section 3.3 ). Figure 2: HCU overview. Top: channels, skill, and action guards. Bottom: a compact AX view, batched actions with a wait step, and the returned effect summary and AX diff. Accessibility for Computer Control AX exposes a structured representation that applications or UI frameworks supply for assistive technologies: a tree of elements with roles, names, values, states, and supported operations. It lets an agent identify and operate controls without locating every target in pixels, but using it to control a computer presents three challenges. 1. Coverage depends on what applications expose. Applications choose which properties and operations to expose through AX. Custom-drawn content may have no accessible elements, accessible objects need not map one-to-one to widgets, and virtualized items may be absent until rendered [ 3 , 24 ] . AX therefore provides incomplete coverage of visible content and available interactions. CUA Driver addresses this by returning the tree and a screenshot together by default, so the model can use pixels when AX omits or misrepresents a target [ 25 ] . HCU retains the acquired AX records, marks unavailable information, and lets the model request a screenshot when semantic evidence is insufficient. 2. Changing targets. Controls can share names, move, disappear, or be recreated; AT-SPI explicitly marks defunct objects [ 26 ] . A label or tree position therefore cannot establish identity across actions. CUA Driver instructs the agent to refresh element indices before acting and rejects ambiguous window targets [ 27 , 28 ] . HCU binds target references independently of the displayed view and resolves them against live elements before each action, including actions within a batch. 3. Verifying action effects. AT-SPI reports invocation, which does not establish that the intended state change occurred [ 29 ] . CUA Driver verifies caller-defined postconditions through a separate operation [ 27 ] . HCU lets the agent compose actions and optional AX wait steps in one batch, such as selecting a checkbox and waiting for its checked state before continuing, without a separate verification call. CUA Driver prioritizes best-effort background input to preserve the user’s active desktop, with foreground input available on request [ 9 ] . In contrast, HCU prioritizes completing the requested action, using native AX operations or focused input as needed. Its efficiency-oriented design also gives the agent more control over how work is composed: compact views reduce observation size, while batched actions, optional wait steps, and AX diffs let the agent combine execution, verification, and state feedback within a single call. Composable Semantic Interaction These properties motivate an AX interface that lets the agent compose actions while HCU validates targets, runs requested wait steps, and returns evidence for continuation. Figure 2 (bottom) illustrates this interaction: a compact AX view supplies target references, a batch combines actions with optional wait steps, and post-action feedback supports the next decision. Compact AX views and target references. HCU separates the AX records it retains from the compact AX view shown to the model. It removes structural wrappers and condenses repeated content in the view while retaining the acquired records for target identification and state comparison. Target references are bound to elements before this compression, so shortening the view does not change which element a reference identifies. The retained records also support AX diffs after an action, while find and scoped observations let the model retrieve targets omitted from the compact AX view. Appendix E.2 gives same-capture examples and measures the reduction in tokens. Batched actions and wait steps. HCU lets the agent compose known actions and optional AX wait steps in a single call. The act mode executes the steps in order within one application window, checking each target with the AX target guard before input (Section 3.2 ). A wait step sends no input and holds until an expected state appears, such as a checkbox becoming checked or a dialog opening, before later steps run; placed last, it verifies the final state. This combines batching, also used for GUI interaction [ 6 ] , with state verification akin to Playwright assertions [ 30 ] . If an action fails, a wait times out, or window continuity is lost, HCU stops the batch and reports the stopping point and execution evidence. This lets the agent decide how to continue without blindly repeating earlier actions. Post-action feedback. HCU returns per-target effect summaries and an AX diff by default after an action call, showing changed values, window changes, and target references relative to the last eligible observation delivered to the model. The agent can instead request a screenshot or execution evidence only, according to what it needs for its next decision. Returning this feedback with the action lets the agent continue without a separate observation when the information suffices (traces and samples in Appendix Figure 16 and E.3 ). HCU reports only what the available evidence supports, so the agent is not led to treat input delivery as a verified effect. Like CUA Driver [ 27 ] , it distinguishes known non-delivery from an unknown effect after possible input. The agent uses this distinction and the returned continuation instructions to decide whether to retry, inspect state, or stop.
