After an action, it may not know which earlier observations remain valid, especially when combining channels. An AX action may open a dialog over coordinates from an earlier screenshot, or a GUI action may replace a control addressed by an AX reference. Reusing that evidence can send input to an unintended target without the model noticing. HCU therefore leaves channel choice to the model while using action guards to check the targets and layouts on which its actions depend immediately before input (Algorithm 1 ). The AX target guard resolves each target reference immediately before execution and checks the element’s identity and action-specific requirements. If the target is missing, ambiguous, or replaced, or an action-specific requirement is not met, HCU rejects the action without sending input. It does not redirect the action to a similarly named element. The GUI layout guard checks whether the layout underlying the model’s chosen coordinates still matches the last screenshot. Before coordinate input, it compares the current desktop bounds, visible top-level windows, stacking order, active window, and target-point window layout with those associated with that screenshot. If the layout has changed, HCU blocks the affected input and returns a fresh screenshot so the model can choose new coordinates. Both guards inspect current state regardless of which channel changed it, including earlier actions in the same channel. Detected mismatches lead to explicit rejection before input, allowing the model to revise its next action (Appendix E.4 ; recorded rejection in Figure 18 ). Skill for Effective Interface Use HCU provides a supplementary skill that explains how to choose and compose the interface’s capabilities. We distilled its instructions from recurring mistakes in development trajectories, including malformed arguments and misused target references, following the trajectory-informed refinement of usage instructions in SWE-agent [ 15 ] . The skill addresses three aspects of interaction: (1) Channel capabilities. The skill explains what programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction can provide, including their observation scope and limitations, so the model can decide which channels to use and combine for the task. (2) Efficient interaction. It explains how to use target references, batch known actions with wait steps, and continue from returned feedback, requesting additional observations only when needed. (3) Verification and recovery. It distinguishes input delivery, local UI changes, and task outcomes; explains how to verify saved or applied results; and describes how to recover from stale targets, invocation errors, or insufficient evidence. The skill makes these instructions concrete through rules for common invocation and recovery mistakes, while the tool schemas define argument shapes. It contains no task-specific solutions; Appendix F.2 presents its text. The skill ablation in Section 4.3 shows reduced invocation errors and improved interaction efficiency; Appendix B.1 describes instruction integration. Experiments Experimental Setup Benchmarks. The main experiment uses the OSWorld 2.0 full set (0808 release; 2 ), and the ablations and cross-model study use OSWorld 1.0 [ 1 ] ; Appendix B.1 lists the task sets. Appendix A reports additional evaluations across OSWorld 1.0, WeaveBench [ 6 ] , MacAgentBench [ 19 ] , and Windows Agent Arena [ 20 ] . Models and comparisons. Each model always runs in the same harness: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.4 in Codex, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, Gemini 3.8 Flash in Gemini CLI, and Grok 4.7 in Grok Build. We therefore name configurations by interface and model. In HCU–CUA Driver comparisons, both interfaces use the same harness execution flow and programmatic tools within each model; auxiliary harness features are restricted to focus the comparison on the interface. The main experiment evaluates HCU (GPT-6 Astra) and HCU (Claude Opus 5) at each model’s highest reasoning effort, with CUA Driver (GPT-6 Astra) as the matched baseline and reported results as context. The interface-component ablations use GPT-5.4 (xhigh); the cross-model comparison adds Claude Opus 5.5 (low), Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and Grok 4.7 (xhigh). We gray out the official GPT-6 Astra results since they were evaluated internally on a subset of tasks. Appendix B.1 details all configurations. Metrics and budgets. We report Partial (mean task score) and Binary (full-credit rate) on OSWorld 2.0 and Score on OSWorld 1.0, along with per-task resource use. The main experiment uses a 500-step limit and the ablations a 100-step limit. We average results across runs within each configuration. Appendix B details the runs, protocols, and metric accounting. Main Results Table 1 compares HCU with results reported by the official OSWorld 2.0 website [ 11 ] , StateAct [ 13 ] , and model vendors [ 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] (Appendix B.2 ). HCU beats the baseline on every measure. HCU scores 3.29 points higher than the baseline while using 29.80% fewer Steps, 56.85% fewer input tokens, 29.85% less Time, and 55.36% lower Cost. Every component contributes to this efficiency: each one cuts Steps by 11–15%, so the full interface needs the fewest Steps of all configurations. Figure 3: Skill effects. AX contributes most. AX is the channel HCU adds to GUI-based computer use: it exposes the applications’ control tree as named, reference-addressed targets and returns observed state changes after action batches. Added to the harness’s programmatic tools and the GUI channel, it raises Score by 2.79 points and cuts Steps by 14.08%, input tokens by 10.44%, Time by 12.58%, and Cost by 10.64%, the largest gain of any component in Score, input, Time, and Cost. The GUI channel complements AX primarily through interaction efficiency: removing GUI leaves Score within run-to-run variation while increasing Steps by 12.45% (Appendix C.1 ). AX thus drives the Score gain and most of the resource savings, while GUI saves Steps when visual context or pixel input is required; Section 4.4 shows how the two divide observation and execution. Execution-centered AX design supports efficient interaction. HCU’s AX channel integrates guarded execution, optional wait steps, and post-action state in one call (Section 3.1.1 ). With only AX and programmatic tools, HCU w/o GUI exceeds CUA Driver by 3.79 points in Score while using 21.06% fewer Steps, 58.33% fewer input tokens, 29.63% less Time, and 56.70% lower Cost. CUA Driver also offers element-addressed actions and separates delivery from effect [ 27 ] , but leaves verification and renewed observation to separate operations. Both interfaces can sequence actions programmatically; HCU builds verification and feedback into the AX call itself. The skill improves calling reliability and interaction efficiency. With the skill (Section 3.3 ), the share of AX and GUI calls rejected for malformed arguments falls from 17.37% to 1.36%, and the share of task-runs that repeat such rejections on the same tool while varying the arguments falls from 44.69% to 0.37% (Figure 3 ). Feedback selection also changes: 87% of AX action calls omit the observe field, selecting the default AX diff, compared with 0.2% without the skill. GUI input actions decrease from 4.96 to 1.97 per task. These behavioral changes accompany a 14.55% reduction in Steps and a 1.59-point gain in Score (Appendix B.1 ). On 29–31% of the tasks where each model used GUI, all GUI calls were screenshots, while the model executed actions through AX (Appendix D.1 ). In one recorded task, a screenshot confirmed an entered value missing from AX feedback, after which the agent continued acting through AX (Appendix D.1 ). Discussion and Conclusion HCU exposes programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction to a general agent and leaves their selection and combination to the model. It achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on OSWorld 2.0, and consistently outperforms CUA Driver in both task performance and efficiency across diverse backbone models, agent harnesses, and desktop platforms. These results suggest that interfaces built on how people operate software, inspecting the screen and using the mouse and keyboard, cost agents both performance and efficiency. Given AX, three of the four models send most of their desktop calls through it (Section 4.4 ). This echoes the bitter lesson [ 35 ] : a strong human-like interface that fixes how the computer is used may limit what increasingly capable models can do with it. The capabilities HCU exposes already exist on standard desktops and require no model retraining. Finally, the AX channel exposes element states that code can read and act on. This makes it possible to treat the desktop as a programmable environment and to bring desktop work into code execution and programmatic tool calling [ 36 ] . HCU’s batched actions with wait steps (Section 3.1.1 ) provide a direct substrate for this composition. We hope this work encourages interfaces that fully leverage what computers already offer to release model capabilities on computer use.
